storySeeds.title: The Scorpius family album
storySeeds.drivingQuestion: Do stars have families, and do siblings age differently?
storySeeds.summary: Start at Seronik's binocular triangle of doubles (β, ν, ω Sco): a real multiple, a hard double-double, and a chance pair. Then δ Sco's disk-driven brightness check against β and π, σ Sco, and Antares: all one 11-Myr Upper Scorpius family, with the heaviest sibling already a red supergiant. Twist: M4 in the same field is about a thousand times older and ten times farther. Coda: τ Sco, still blue, possibly a merger.

storySeeds.drivingQuestion: Can you trust how bright, or how close together, stars look?
storySeeds.summary: ε Sco looks like Antares' near-twin but is nine times nearer. μ¹/μ² is a naked-eye pair of real neighbors (and μ¹ eclipses), while ζ¹/ζ² is a perspective trick: orange ζ² at 135 ly, blue ζ¹ a hypergiant near 5,500 ly in NGC 6231, the 'head' of Wedel's False Comet. Finish at Shaula's weighed triple and the naked-eye cluster M7.

storySeeds.title: Methuselah, the Sun's twin and the Sun's future
storySeeds.region: Libra, Serpens Caput and western Ophiuchus (≈25° patch)
storySeeds.drivingQuestion: How old can a star be, and what will happen to the Sun?
storySeeds.summary: From 'green' Zubeneschamali hop to HD 140283, a 12-Gyr halo subgiant with 1/250 of the Sun's metals, then M5, a globular of similar age. 18 Sco shows the Sun as it is today, Yed Prior the red-giant stage ahead, and 36 Oph three smaller orange suns only 19 ly away. Uses the NASA/Hubble 'Methuselah' story and the Bazot asteroseismic twin result.

storySeeds.title: The Teapot in 3-D, pointing at the Galaxy's heart
storySeeds.region: Sagittarius Teapot and the Lagoon (≈15° patch)
storySeeds.drivingQuestion: How deep is the sky behind a flat-looking asterism?
storySeeds.summary: Teapot stars at 78 (Kaus Borealis), 143 (Kaus Australis), 348 (Kaus Media) and 97 ly (Alnasl) show the asterism is a perspective picture; the spout points 4.6° from the hidden Galactic Center. Then 9 Sgr, the ~1-Myr O-star pair energizing the Lagoon at ~4,300 ly, and Ascella beside M54, a cluster from the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy. Pairs well with an R Scuti/δ Scuti variable-star coda near M11 (Astronomy magazine's R Sct guide).

card.question: How can a star cooler than the Sun outshine it tens of thousands of times?
card.glance: The orange-red heart of Scorpius; in binoculars a vivid ember with a faint round globular cluster beside it.
card.whyHere: Scorpius is one big family of stars born about 11 million years ago, and Antares is the sibling that has raced ahead to old age.
card.see: Antares glows low in the south as the red heart of Scorpius. Put it near the edge of the field and its orange deepens, especially if you defocus slightly; about two and a half Moon-widths to the west sits M4, a soft round gray glow.
card.understand: Antares was born perhaps 15 times heavier than the Sun, and heavy stars burn their fuel recklessly fast, so it has already used up its core hydrogen and swollen into a supergiant. Its surface has cooled to about 3,700 degrees against the Sun's 5,800, which is why it glows orange-red. In 2017 astronomers mapped gas rising and sinking across that vast surface.
card.wonder: Antares is heavy enough to end as a supernova, probably within the next hundred thousand years or so.
card.connect: τ Scorpii, two degrees away, is a sibling still hot and blue.
card.answer: Antares wins by sheer size: about 680 times wider than the Sun, so although each patch of its surface is dimmer than the Sun's, the total comes to tens of thousands of Suns. Swap it for the Sun and its surface would reach beyond the orbit of Mars.
card.photoCaption: ESO's interferometer turned Antares into a lumpy disk of hot and cool patches; the survey photo shows only a saturated point beside M4.
card.notSee: The surface detail and the blue companion about 3 arcseconds away are far beyond binoculars.
card.deeper: Ohnaka et al. (2013) measured a limb-darkened diameter of 37.4 milliarcseconds with ESO's VLTI and derived 3,660 ± 120 K and log L/L☉ = 4.88 ± 0.23. At the Hipparcos 2007 distance (≈170 pc, ±17%) that angle means a radius near 680 R☉; the radius scales with the still-uncertain distance. Pecaut et al. (2012) included Antares when revising the Upper Scorpius age to 11 ± 1 ± 2 Myr. Mass estimates of 12–15 M☉ put it well above the ~8 M☉ needed to end as a core-collapse supernova, probably within the next hundred thousand years or so.

vsiniKms.note: very slow rotator; magnetic rotation period 41.033 d (Donati et al. 2006)

card.question: Why is one sibling red and swollen while another stays small and blue?
card.glance: A plain blue-white point just south-east of Antares; the color contrast with its neighbor is the show.
card.whyHere: If Antares is the family member grown old, τ Scorpii, born from the same cloud at the same time, is the one who still looks young, and the reason lies at the heart of how stars live.
card.see: Put Antares at one edge of a wide field and sweep about two degrees south-east, toward the tail of Scorpius. Swing back and forth between them, deep orange against crisp blue-white, and defocus both slightly to judge the colors as small disks.
card.understand: τ's surface is about 31,000 degrees, five times hotter than the Sun's and eight times hotter than Antares'. A star's mass sets its pace: the heavier it is, the harder gravity squeezes its core and the faster it burns. Antares started heavier and has already exhausted its core hydrogen, while τ, lighter, is still in its long, steady middle life.
card.wonder: It spins remarkably slowly, about once every six weeks, and carries a tangled magnetic field that single-star models struggle to explain.
card.connect: Dschubba, in the head of Scorpius, is a sibling that grew a disk.
card.answer: The two share a birthday but not a weight, and the heavier sibling simply lives faster. τ even looks younger than its own family, perhaps because it was once two stars that merged and reset its clock.
card.photoCaption: No photograph resolves τ; the in-app swatch places its color beside Antares' on one temperature scale.
card.deeper: Keszthelyi et al. (2021) fitted its spectrum with CMFGEN: Teff = 31,500 ± 1,000 K, log g = 4.2 and log L/L☉ = 4.56 ± 0.20. It rotates slowly (41-day magnetic period; Donati et al. 2006) and carries an unusually complex surface magnetic field and extra nitrogen. Single-star models struggle to reproduce all of this; the authors favor a merger or other binary history, which would also explain why it looks younger than the 11-Myr Upper Scorpius group it belongs to.

historyHook.text: In mid-2000, as its companion swung in close, δ Sco began shedding a disk of gas and changed the familiar look of Scorpius' head.

card.question: How can a star suddenly grow a disk of gas and brighten?
card.glance: The middle star of the arc at Scorpius' head; a bright white point whose brightness has wandered since 2000.
card.whyHere: Stars change over millions of years, so it is rare to watch one transform within a human lifetime, and δ Scorpii did exactly that in the year 2000.
card.see: δ is the middle star of the short upright arc forming Scorpius' head, north-west of Antares. Compare it with β above and π below: is δ clearly the brightest, or about equal? Your answer is a real measurement, since its disk has made it vary for two decades.
card.understand: δ Sco is a hot, heavy star spinning so fast that gas at its equator is barely held on. When a companion on a stretched 11-year orbit swung in close in 2000, the star began shedding a flat disk of gas around its waist. Hot stars with such disks are called Be stars, the e for the glow of the disk gas, which adds light of its own.
card.wonder: At closest approach its companion dives to within about 15 times δ's own radius.
card.connect: Acrab, just above it, hides a whole family in one point.
card.answer: Spinning near its limit, it was tipped over by a close pass of its companion: since 2000 δ Scorpii has worn a glowing ring of gas that changes how bright it looks, and the familiar shape of the Scorpion's head changed within living memory.
card.photoCaption: No image resolves the disk; the light-curve sketch shows the shape of its slow, irregular changes, not a forecast.
card.notSee: The disk itself is far too small to see; only its effect on the star's brightness reaches your eye.
card.deeper: Miroshnichenko et al. (2001) followed the onset of strong Hα emission and enhanced mass loss just before the 2000 periastron, when the stars come within ~15 primary radii. Their study of the 2011 periastron (2011 July 3) refined the orbit to 10.8092 ± 0.0005 yr, adopted a distance of 136 pc and estimated a disk radius of ~150 R☉ (Miroshnichenko et al. 2013). The GCVS range (V 1.86–2.32) predates the outburst; treat any printed magnitude as historical and compare with β and π Sco on the night.

eventDependent.note: Its disk makes its brightness drift over months and years; compare it with β and π Scorpii tonight rather than trusting a printed value.

card.question: How many stars can hide in a single point of light?
card.glance: The top star of Scorpius' head: one point hand-held, though a steady 10× view may show a close companion.
card.whyHere: Scorpius is a family of young stars, and Acrab shows that inside the big family are smaller ones, nested like rooms within a house.
card.see: Brace your binoculars or use a tripod, and at 10× or more look for a fainter star hugging β on its north-north-east side, about a third of Jupiter's width away. Hand-held, most people see one star, and that is normal.
card.understand: The two stars you may split share one distance and drift through space together, so they are true partners. Each of them is itself a tight pair, revealed when the Moon passes in front and the light winks out in steps, or by telescopes that combine light from several mirrors. Heavy stars are usually born in groups like this, and watching partners orbit is how astronomers weigh them.
card.wonder: The light reaching you left around the time Galileo first turned a telescope on the sky.
card.connect: ν Scorpii, one and a half degrees east, is a tougher double.
card.answer: At least five in Acrab: binoculars may split two, and each of those is itself a tight pair. What looks like one bright star is a small family of its own.
card.photoCaption: The in-app binocular field shows the pair at true separation; whether you can split it depends on magnification and a steady mount.
card.notSee: The inner pairs of β¹ and β², found by lunar occultations and interferometry, are invisible in any small instrument.
card.deeper: WDS lists AC at 13.7″ (PA 19°, V 2.6 and 4.5) from Herschel's 1779 measures through 2021, a close AB pair at 0.3″, and occultation pairs inside both A and C. The β¹ and β² Hipparcos/Gaia parallaxes agree (8.07 ± 0.78 and 8.24 ± 0.50 mas). Sky & Telescope's Binocular Highlight (Seronik 2015) groups β, ν and ω Sco as one triangle of binocular doubles. Practical limit: about 30″ hand-held at 10×, so treat AC as a mounted-binocular challenge.

card.question: Can a faint speck beside a star be a whole system of its own?
card.glance: A modest star east of β Scorpii; a steady 10× view can tease out a faint companion.
card.whyHere: Next to Acrab sits Scorpius' own version of the Double-Double, two pairs of stars circling each other.
card.see: From β, nudge about one and a half degrees east-north-east to ν. On a tripod at 10× or more, a much fainter star sits just north-north-west of it, roughly one Jupiter-width away; hand-held, the companion usually drowns in the glare.
card.understand: Telescopes show that each of the two stars you can split is itself a close pair, and the brightest is a tighter pair still. That makes at least five suns, all born with Scorpius' blue-white stars about eleven million years ago. Gaia confirms that the bright star and its faint neighbor sit at the same distance.
card.wonder: The light you see left it nearly five centuries ago, around when Copernicus was moving the Sun to the center of the planets.
card.connect: ω Scorpii, just south, is a pair that is no family at all.
card.answer: The speck beside ν Scorpii is just that, a double star in its own right, so a glance that shows you two stars is really looking at a crowd. It is the hardest of the three binocular doubles in the Scorpion's head, and the most rewarding.
card.photoCaption: The binocular-field drawing shows the 41-arcsecond pair at your magnification; photos are needed to show the close inner pairs.
card.notSee: Both inner pairs (1.3″ and 2.4″) need a telescope.
card.deeper: WDS: AC 41.4″ at PA 336° (V 4.35 and 6.6), AB 1.3″, CD 2.4″, and Aa,Ab resolved by speckle at 0.1″. Seronik (Sky & Telescope, June 2015) calls the AC split a serious binocular challenge that needs mounted binoculars of 10× or more because of the brightness difference. Gaia parallaxes of A and C agree (≈7.1–7.3 mas), consistent with one physical system in the Upper Scorpius group.

card.question: Are two stars side by side always a real pair?
card.glance: Two similar stars a quarter-degree apart just south of β Scorpii; easy in any binoculars, with a gentle color contrast.
card.whyHere: After two real families, here is a pair that only pretends, a useful lesson in how deep the sky really is.
card.see: From β, drop about one degree south. Two stars of similar brightness sit about half a Moon-width apart, easy even at 7×, and sharp eyes split them without optics; the north-western one is blue-white, the other faintly yellow.
card.understand: Distance and motion are how astronomers tell real pairs from chance ones. Gaia puts blue-white ω¹, a hot young member of the Scorpius family, about 460 light-years away. Yellow ω² is an older giant only about 290 light-years off, drifting across the sky in a completely different direction.
card.wonder: From a planet circling ω¹, the yellow star would be some 170 light-years away and nowhere near it in the sky.
card.connect: The bright stars of Scorpius' head, by contrast, were born together.
card.answer: These two merely line up from where we stand, one far behind the other and each going its own way.
card.photoCaption: The in-app distance bar puts the two stars at their true depths: side by side on the sky, far apart in space.
card.deeper: Gaia DR3 parallaxes: ω¹ (B1 V) 7.10 ± 0.27 mas, ω² (G4 II-III) 11.15 ± 0.16 mas, i.e. about 460 and 292 ly. Proper motions differ strongly (ω¹ −10, −23 mas/yr; ω² +42, −45 mas/yr), so this is an optical pair. ω¹ is a classic Upper Scorpius member (de Zeeuw et al. 1999). Separation ≈14.6′, PA 145°.

card.question: What makes a star dip in brightness every day and a half?
card.glance: A naked-eye pair of blue-white stars in the curl of Scorpius' tail; the brighter one quietly dips every day and a half.
card.whyHere: Some stars change because of what happens inside them and some because of the company they keep, and μ¹ Scorpii is two stars so close they almost touch.
card.see: Follow the tail of Scorpius down from Antares to where it starts to curl. μ¹ and μ² sit about a fifth of a Moon-width apart, a naked-eye pair that binoculars widen into two blue-white points; use μ² as your yardstick, since some nights μ¹ looks clearly brighter and others almost equal.
card.understand: μ¹ is two hot stars whirling around each other every 35 hours, so close that one has swollen to fill its share of space and spills gas onto its partner. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so on every lap each star passes in front of the other. Astronomers call this an eclipsing binary, and its light curve is a record of the orbit.
card.wonder: To complete an orbit in about a day and a half, their surfaces race along at hundreds of kilometers per second.
card.connect: Farther down the tail, ζ Scorpii is a naked-eye pair that is a complete illusion.
card.answer: Eclipses do it, for on every orbit each star blocks part of the other and the combined light dips by about a fifth.
card.photoCaption: The light-curve sketch shows the shape of μ¹'s double dip per orbit; it is a typical shape, not a forecast.
card.notSee: The two stars of μ¹ are far too close to separate; you only see their combined light change.
card.deeper: GCVS classes μ¹ Sco as EB/SD (a semi-detached β Lyrae-type system), V 2.94–3.22, P = 1.4462691 d, spectral types B1.5 V + B6.5 V. Hipparcos 2007 puts it near 150 pc, inside Upper Centaurus–Lupus; Gaia's single-star solution (1.9 ± 0.7 mas) is unreliable for such a bright, close binary. μ² (B2 IV) lies 5.8′ away at about 177 pc. The two share Sco-Cen motion, but no orbit links them.

card.question: Can a faint-looking star be one of the brightest in the Galaxy?
card.glance: The fainter, paler star of a naked-eye pair low in Scorpius' tail, with a sparkling cluster just north.
card.whyHere: Brightness in the sky can deceive badly, and ζ¹ Scorpii is the most extreme case in the summer sky: one of the most luminous stars the eye can see, disguised as a faint one.
card.see: Where the tail bends south, two stars sit a few arcminutes apart, an easy naked-eye pair: orange ζ² and the fainter, paler ζ¹. Half a degree north lies a tight knot of stars, the cluster NGC 6231; from mid-northern sites this scene hugs the horizon and needs a clear southern view.
card.understand: Orange ζ² is a nearby giant about 135 light-years away, while ζ¹, a hot blue star that dust along the way tints pale yellow-white, lies roughly forty times farther, in NGC 6231. Forty times the distance means sixteen hundred times less light, so for ζ¹ to look even roughly as bright as its neighbor it must be a monster. It is a hypergiant, an unstable, swollen stage only the heaviest stars reach.
card.wonder: The light reaching you tonight left it before anyone on Earth had learned to write.
card.connect: NGC 6231, the family it came from, sits right beside it.
card.answer: ζ¹ Scorpii is one, shining with nearly a million Suns and looking faint only because it is about 5,500 light-years away. Moved to ζ²'s distance, it would outshine every star in our night sky by far.
card.photoCaption: ESO's wide photograph shows NGC 6231's blue stars and the red glow around them, color your eye will not see.
card.notSee: The surrounding red nebulosity in photographs is invisible in binoculars.
card.deeper: Clark et al. (2012) modeled ζ¹ Sco with non-LTE atmospheres: at an adopted 1.64 kpc, Teff = 17.2 kK, log L/L☉ = 5.93, R = 103 R☉ and a spectroscopic mass of 36 M☉ (53 M☉ and log L = 6.10 at 1.99 kpc). Its properties lie between blue supergiants and luminous blue variables. Gaia DR3 gives 0.59 ± 0.12 mas (≈1.4–2.1 kpc). It has been photometrically stable since 1949. ζ² (K3 III, 24.2 mas) is an unrelated foreground giant.

card.question: What happens to a star when its partner explodes?
card.glance: A lone blue-white star in southern Ophiuchus; plain in binoculars, but its story is one of the best in the sky.
card.whyHere: Heavy stars rarely live alone, and ζ Ophiuchi is a survivor: its partner exploded, and the blast flung it clean out of the Scorpius family.
card.see: Look about 16° north of Antares, in Ophiuchus, for a lone bright star in a fairly empty field. It is a clean blue-white point with no cluster and no family around it, which is exactly the point.
card.understand: About 20 times heavier than the Sun, ζ Oph was once half of a close pair in the Scorpius–Centaurus family. When its even heavier partner exploded as a supernova, the gravity holding the pair together vanished in an instant, and ζ Oph flew off like a stone from a sling. Run its Gaia motion backward and it leads to the same spot as a pulsar, the collapsed core of its old partner.
card.wonder: Some astronomers tie that explosion, about 1.8 million years ago, to radioactive iron atoms found on Earth.
card.connect: Antares has not exploded yet; when it does, it will scatter its own neighbors.
card.answer: It can be set loose: ζ Ophiuchi lost its partner to a supernova and now races alone through space, its fierce wind piling interstellar dust into a glowing arc ahead of it like a ship's bow wave.
card.photoCaption: Spitzer's infrared and Chandra's X-ray light reveal the bow shock and hot gas; your eyes see only the star.
card.notSee: The bow shock and the hot X-ray bubble are invisible to the eye at any aperture.
card.deeper: Neuhäuser et al. (2020) traced ζ Oph and the pulsar PSR B1706−16 back with Gaia DR2 to a common origin in Upper Centaurus–Lupus, 1.78 ± 0.21 Myr ago at about 107 pc, and linked the same supernova to ⁶⁰Fe deposited on Earth. An older study (Hoogerwerf et al. 2001) preferred an Upper Scorpius origin with a different pulsar, so the details remain debated. The distance is uncertain: Hipparcos 2007 gives 112 ± 3 pc, Gaia DR3 about 135 pc. 'nn' in its spectral type marks very broad lines from extremely fast rotation.

superlatives.claim: one of the closest known matches to the Sun

card.question: What would our Sun look like from a few dozen light-years away?
card.glance: A faint yellow-white point south of the Yed pair in Ophiuchus, ordinary because it is almost a copy of our Sun.
card.whyHere: To know whether the Sun is special, it helps to find its twin, and 18 Scorpii matches it in size, mass and temperature almost exactly.
card.see: Start at δ and ε Ophiuchi, the close naked-eye pair called Yed, and sweep about five degrees south. 18 Sco is the brightest star in a modest field, a soft yellow-white point just visible to the eye under dark skies; compare its tint with blue-white ζ Ophiuchi about six degrees east.
card.understand: Its width was measured by combining telescopes into one sharp eye, and its mass came from the way its surface quivers as sound waves ring through the star. Both came out within a few percent of the Sun's, and its temperature is within a few dozen degrees. Like the Sun, it quietly fuses hydrogen into helium deep inside.
card.wonder: Twins like this are how astronomers test whether the Sun is a typical star or an unusual one.
card.connect: HD 140283, in Libra, is a Sun-like star from when the Galaxy was young.
card.answer: Much like 18 Scorpii does tonight, a faint yellow-white point 46 light-years away, easy to overlook without a dark sky. From there our Sun would be just such an unremarkable star, a humbling thought on a summer night.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the size comparison draws 18 Sco and the Sun as near-identical disks.
card.deeper: Bazot et al. (2011) combined HARPS asteroseismology (large frequency separation 134.4 ± 0.3 μHz) with CHARA/PAVO interferometry (limb-darkened diameter 0.676 ± 0.006 mas) to get R = 1.010 ± 0.009 R☉ and M = 1.02 ± 0.03 M☉. Its Gaia benchmark temperature is 5,810 ± 80 K (Heiter et al. 2015). Model ages disagree (a later analysis found a two-peaked solution near 4.7 and 7 Gyr), so no age is quoted. Gaia DR3 parallax: 70.74 ± 0.06 mas.

distanceLy.note: Gaia DR3 16.267 ± 0.026 mas; HST FGS 17.15 ± 0.14 mas (Bond et al. 2013)

ageMyr.note: 12.0 ± 0.5 Gyr incl. modelling uncertainty (earlier 14.46 ± 0.8 Gyr, Bond et al. 2013)

teffK.note: Gaia benchmark value, flagged as uncertain

superlatives.claim: one of the oldest stars with a well-measured age

historyHook.text: When Hubble pinned down its distance in 2013, the first age came out near 14.5 billion years, uncomfortably close to the age of the Universe.

card.question: How old can a star in our own neighborhood be?
card.glance: A faint, unremarkable point in western Libra that needs a careful hop: one of the oldest stars you will ever see.
card.whyHere: Most nearby stars are the Sun's contemporaries, but a few are visitors from the Galaxy's youth, and HD 140283 is the most famous of them.
card.see: Hop about six and a half degrees east of Zubeneschamali (β Librae) and use the chart to pick out a faint, slightly yellow point among similar stars. There is nothing special to see; the wonder is in knowing what it is.
card.understand: Its atoms are a birth certificate: it holds only about a 250th of the Sun's share of elements heavier than helium, so it formed before many generations of stars had enriched the Galaxy's gas. In 2013 Hubble measured its distance precisely, which fixes its true brightness, and models of how such stars age gave a first answer near 14.5 billion years, awkwardly older than the Universe. Better models and a measured radius later brought it down.
card.wonder: When the Sun and Earth formed, this star was already more than seven billion years old.
card.connect: Globular clusters such as M4 gather stars of the same vintage in crowds.
card.answer: About 12 billion years, give or take half a billion: HD 140283 formed when the Galaxy was young and nearly free of heavy elements. It moves fast on a long, tilted orbit through the halo, perhaps born in a small galaxy the Milky Way later swallowed.
card.photoCaption: The age bar places it against the Sun and the Universe; the survey field shows a plain 7th-magnitude star.
card.deeper: Bond et al. (2013) measured a parallax of 17.15 ± 0.14 mas with Hubble's Fine Guidance Sensors and derived 14.46 ± 0.8 Gyr. Tang & Joyce (2021) revised this with MESA models and an interferometric radius to 12.0 ± 0.5 Gyr and 0.81 ± 0.05 M☉, removing the tension with the 13.8-Gyr Universe. [Fe/H] ≈ −2.4. Gaia DR3 gives 16.27 ± 0.03 mas (≈200 ly) and a proper motion of 1.16″/yr; radial velocity −170 km/s. Its benchmark temperature (5,522 ± 105 K) is flagged as uncertain.

distanceLy.note: Gaia DR3 parallax of A 168.00 ± 0.13 mas; C 167.96 ± 0.03 mas

multiplicity.systemNote: Three orange dwarfs: a close AB binary and a wide companion C 12′ away with the same parallax and motion.

card.question: Why do some of our nearest neighbors look so faint?
card.glance: An orange point in southern Ophiuchus with a fainter orange companion a fifth of a degree away: a three-star family next door.
card.whyHere: At about 19 light-years, 36 Ophiuchi is one of the closest star systems you can easily see, and it makes a perfect contrast with the giants of Scorpius nearby.
card.see: 36 Oph lies about ten degrees east of Antares, a few degrees east of the globular clusters M19 and M62. Look for a fainter orange star about a fifth of a degree to its east-north-east: that is 36 Oph C, a true family member.
card.understand: All three stars are orange dwarfs, a little smaller and cooler than the Sun, sharing one distance and drifting together. Gaia measures their distances to within a fraction of a percent, and they agree. Antares, nearly thirty times farther, still outshines them because it is a giant: a lighthouse far away against a candle close by.
card.wonder: The light you see left only about 19 years ago, within living memory for almost everyone.
card.connect: M19 and M62, just west, are about a thousand times farther.
card.answer: Because most stars are modest: 36 Ophiuchi's three orange dwarfs give out little light, so even at 19 light-years they look unremarkable. The brightest stars in the sky are rarely the nearest; they are the powerful ones.
card.photoCaption: The binocular-field drawing shows A and C at their true separation; the AB pair is drawn as one point.
card.notSee: The 5-arcsecond AB pair needs a telescope.
card.deeper: Gaia DR3 parallaxes: A 168.00 ± 0.13 mas and C 167.96 ± 0.03 mas (19.4 ly), with matching proper motions near 1.2″/yr. WDS lists AB at 5.1″ (K2 V + K1 V, both V ≈ 5.1) and C (K5 V, V 6.3–6.5) at 732″, which is about 4,400 au in projection. A fourth WDS entry (D, 295″, V 7.8) is not known to be related.

distanceLy.note: 1.31 ± 0.06 kpc from the visual + spectroscopic orbit

multiplicity.systemNote: Interferometric + spectroscopic binary: P = 8.9 ± 0.2 yr, e = 0.648 (Fabry et al. 2021).

historyHook.text: Its two stars are so evenly matched that it took until the 2010s to prove it was a binary at all.

images.caption: VST image of the Lagoon Nebula; 9 Sgr is among the bright stars in the glowing gas.

card.question: What makes the Lagoon Nebula glow?
card.glance: The bright white star inside the Lagoon Nebula's glow, above the spout of the Teapot.
card.whyHere: Every glowing nebula needs a lamp, and in the Lagoon the lamp is visible: a young pair of giant stars sitting right in the mist.
card.see: Find the Lagoon Nebula above the spout of the Teapot in Sagittarius. A bright star sits right in the misty glow, 9 Sgr, with the loose cluster NGC 6530 just east; expect gray mist rather than the pink of photographs, since night vision sees almost no color.
card.understand: 9 Sgr looked like one star until the 2010s, because its two members are so evenly matched. Telescopes that combine light from several mirrors finally separated them: two of the heaviest kind of star, about 53 and 39 times the Sun's mass, circling every nine years. Stars this heavy are fiercely hot and flood their surroundings with ultraviolet light.
card.wonder: When the pair began to shine, our own ancestors were already walking the Earth.
card.connect: NGC 6530, beside it, shares its birthplace.
card.answer: That ultraviolet light strips electrons from the hydrogen around 9 Sagittarii, and as they rejoin their atoms the gas glows, much like a neon sign. The pair is only about a million years old, so the Lagoon is lit by stars that are newborns themselves.
card.photoCaption: ESO's VST photo records the red hydrogen glow and dark lanes that long exposures collect; binoculars show gray mist around 9 Sgr.
card.notSee: The red color and fine dust lanes of the photo are beyond the eye.
card.deeper: Fabry et al. (2021) resolved the pair with VLTI PIONIER and GRAVITY and disentangled its spectra: an O3.5 V((f+)) primary of ≈53 M☉ and an O5–5.5 V((f)) secondary of ≈39 M☉ on an 8.9 ± 0.2 yr, e = 0.65 orbit, at 1.31 ± 0.06 kpc, both about 1 Myr old. The Lagoon review by Tothill et al. (2008) treats 9 Sgr as the main ionizing source of much of the visible nebula. Whether it is a full member of NGC 6530 is still discussed.

distanceLy.note: Gaia DR3 2.535 ± 0.087 mas; parallax of a large pulsating star may be biased

periodDays.note: interval between deep minima; behaviour irregular

card.question: Why does this star fade unevenly, sometimes almost to nothing?
card.glance: A yellowish star just north-west of the Wild Duck Cluster whose brightness swings irregularly.
card.whyHere: Late in life some stars lose their rhythm, and R Scuti is the brightest example, a giant whose breathing stumbles.
card.see: Find M11, the Wild Duck Cluster in Scutum, then look about one degree north-west for a yellowish star in a small group. Near its best it is easy, while in a deep dip it is a faint speck, so check again in a week: it never repeats exactly.
card.understand: R Sct has used up its core hydrogen and swollen into a cool, bloated giant whose outer layers pulse unevenly. Deep and shallow dips alternate, with roughly 146 days between the deep ones, and sometimes the rhythm stalls altogether. Stars in this unsettled phase shed gas that may one day form a glowing shell.
card.wonder: At its best it is a naked-eye star, and at its worst you need binoculars and a chart to find it at all.
card.connect: δ Scuti, a few degrees away, pulses in hours, not months.
card.answer: Its pulsations are uneven, the giant's loose outer layers swinging between deep and shallow dips, at times dimming it fiftyfold before it recovers over a couple of months.
card.photoCaption: The light-curve sketch shows the RV Tauri pattern of alternating deep and shallow dips: a typical shape, not a forecast.
card.deeper: GCVS classes R Sct as RVa: V 4.2–8.6 with about 146.5 days between deep minima. Astronomy magazine's guide describes maxima near 4.5–5.0, shallow minima of 6.5–7.0 and deep minima of 8–9, and suggests checking it every 5–7 nights. Kipper & Klochkova (2013) found Teff ≈ 4,500 K and [Fe/H] ≈ −0.5; whether it is still on the AGB or has left it is debated. Gaia DR3 gives 2.54 ± 0.09 mas (≈1,300 ly), which may be biased for such a large pulsating star.

eventDependent.note: Its brightness changes irregularly from week to week; compare it with nearby stars or check AAVSO rather than relying on a listed magnitude.

superlatives.claim: prototype of the δ Scuti class of rapidly pulsating stars

card.question: Can a star ring like a bell several times a day?
card.glance: A modest white star south-west of the Wild Duck Cluster that pulses every 4 hours 39 minutes, far too subtly to see.
card.whyHere: R Scuti breathes over months, but δ Scuti nearby vibrates in hours, the namesake of a whole class of quick-pulsing stars.
card.see: From M11 in Scutum, slide about three and a half degrees south-west to δ Scuti, a white point. Watch it for a few minutes and you will see no change, because its light rises and falls by only about a sixth, far below what eyes can judge in one sitting.
card.understand: δ Scuti is a little heavier than the Sun and near the end of its steady hydrogen-burning life. Its outer layers vibrate in several rhythms at once, like a bell struck in a few places, the main one every 4 hours 39 minutes. Each rhythm reaches a different depth, so timing them lets astronomers probe the star's insides, as earthquakes reveal what lies beneath Earth's crust.
card.wonder: Its beat is measured in hours, while R Scuti, a few degrees away, takes about five months for one cycle.
card.connect: R Scuti, beside M11, pulses in changes you can actually see.
card.answer: It can, and δ Scuti's main beat comes round about five times a day, too subtle for the eye yet carrying a map of the star's interior.
card.photoCaption: The light-curve sketch exaggerates its tiny ripple; real changes are about a fifth of a magnitude.
card.deeper: GCVS: type DSCT, V 4.60–4.79, main period 0.1937697 d (4.65 h); the star pulsates in several modes at once, which is the basis of asteroseismology of this class. Gaia DR3 parallax 16.19 ± 0.12 mas (≈201 ly). Its spectrum (F2 II-III, peculiar) places it in the instability strip just above the main sequence.

multiplicity.systemNote: Wide common-proper-motion pair; WDS also lists close faint components around both stars.

card.question: Do two stars that look close really travel together?
card.glance: Libra's southern claw: a bright white star with a fainter companion clearly separate in any binoculars.
card.whyHere: Libra's southern claw is the easiest double in this part of the sky, and unlike many pretty pairs, this one is genuine.
card.see: Find Libra between Virgo's Spica and Antares. Center Zubenelgenubi and look just north-west, where a fainter star stands clearly apart, about an eighth of a Moon-width away; it is easy even at 7×, and the bright star is white, the companion a touch creamier.
card.understand: To test a pair, astronomers check whether both stars sit at the same distance and drift across the sky together. These do: both are about 76 light-years away and moving side by side. The brighter star is itself a tight pair that only its spectrum reveals.
card.wonder: From either star, the other would shine far brighter than any star in our sky, yet still as a single point.
card.connect: Zubeneschamali, the other claw nine degrees north-east, is the star some call green.
card.answer: These two do, though at a stately pace: their gap is more than 5,000 times the Earth–Sun distance, so one orbit, if they complete one at all, would take well over a hundred thousand years.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo matches the binocular view well: two separate points of different brightness.
card.deeper: WDS: AB 230.8″ at PA 314° (2016), V 2.74 and 5.19 (SHJ 186). Parallaxes agree (Hipparcos 2007 α² 43.03 ± 0.19 mas; Gaia DR3 α¹ 41.77 ± 0.38 mas), and proper motions are similar once α²'s orbital wobble is allowed for. The projected separation is about 5,400 au. WDS also lists a spectroscopic pair inside α² and a faint close companion of α¹.

superlatives.claim: often called the only naked-eye green star, though most observers see it blue-white

card.question: Can a star really look green?
card.glance: Libra's northern claw, a blue-white star that some observers insist looks green; defocus it and decide.
card.whyHere: Here is a star that lets your own eyes join an old argument: it is often called the only green star, though physics says it should not be.
card.see: Center Zubeneschamali and defocus slightly so it becomes a small disk. Compare it with white Zubenelgenubi nine degrees south-west and, if it is up, orange Antares low in the south-east, and decide before reading on: green tinge, pale blue, or plain white?
card.understand: Its surface is about 12,000 degrees, twice as hot as the Sun's, so its light leans blue and it should look blue-white. A glowing body never emits just one color; it pours out a broad spread of them, and even a star whose output peaked in green would send plenty of red and blue too. Our eyes blend that mixture into white, which is why the Sun, whose light peaks near green, looks white from space.
card.wonder: Observers have argued about this star's color for generations, and tonight your eyes cast a vote.
card.connect: δ Librae, nearby, is a star that winks.
card.answer: No star truly does, because a star's light is always a broad mix, and a mix centered on green looks white. Zubeneschamali is blue-white, and any green you see comes from contrast with nearby colors and the way our eyes handle color in dim light.
card.photoCaption: The swatch shows its computed color, blue-white; compare that with what your eye reported.
card.deeper: BBC Sky at Night summarizes the case: a B8 V star of about 12,300 K and roughly 80 Myr, often described in older literature as greenish, while most modern observers report blue-white; there is no accepted physical explanation for a green appearance. The 'n' in B8Vn marks broad lines from fast rotation. Hipparcos 2007 parallax 17.62 ± 0.16 mas (≈185 ly).

distanceLy.note: Hipparcos 2007 11.11 ± 0.60 mas; Gaia DR3 9.28 ± 0.47 mas (≈350 ly)

card.question: How can you watch one star pass in front of another?
card.glance: A modest white star in Libra that loses more than half its light for part of a night every 2.3 days.
card.whyHere: Most eclipsing stars dip too little to notice, but δ Librae loses more than half its light, a wink you can actually catch.
card.see: δ Lib sits about eight degrees north-north-east of Zubenelgenubi. Compare it with neighboring stars of similar brightness, ideally on two nights: usually it holds steady, but during an eclipse it looks clearly fainter, and the app's eclipse list tells you whether tonight is a good night.
card.understand: δ Lib is an eclipsing binary, two stars orbiting every 2 days and 8 hours, far too close for any telescope to split. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so once per lap the dimmer star slides in front of the brighter one and blocks much of its light. Gas also streams from one star onto the other, slowly reshaping both.
card.wonder: Each eclipse lasts hours, so on a good night you can watch the star fade and recover before bedtime.
card.connect: μ¹ Scorpii, in the tail of Scorpius, plays the same game with a smaller dip.
card.answer: Watch δ Librae at the right hour: every 2.3 days its fainter star slides across the brighter one and the light drops by more than half, a shadow play staged about 300 light-years away on a schedule predictable to within minutes.
card.photoCaption: The light-curve sketch shows a flat line with a sharp dip each orbit: the classic eclipsing pattern.
card.notSee: The two stars are never seen separately; only their combined light changes.
card.deeper: GCVS: EA/SD (Algol type, semi-detached), V 4.91–5.90, P = 2.3273543 d, epoch JD 2442960.6994, spectral type A0 IV-V. Hipparcos 2007 gives 11.11 ± 0.60 mas (≈290 ly) and Gaia DR3 9.28 ± 0.47 mas (≈350 ly); the difference may reflect the binary's orbital motion. Predicted minima drift if the period changes, so a recent ephemeris is better than the GCVS epoch for timing.

eventDependent.note: Eclipses repeat every 2.33 days; the star looks normal most of the time, so check a predicted-minimum time before comparing.

card.question: Why does a far smaller star look almost as bright as Antares?
card.glance: The bright orange-yellow star where the tail of Scorpius starts to curve, south-south-east of Antares.
card.whyHere: Two orange stars of nearly equal brightness sit in Scorpius, and comparing them is one of the clearest lessons in how distance fools the eye.
card.see: Drop about nine degrees south-south-east from Antares to the first bright star of the tail. Put each in the field in turn: ε is paler, more yellow-orange, and Antares a deeper orange, yet they are close in brightness.
card.understand: ε Sco is about 64 light-years away and Antares roughly 550, nearly nine times farther. Light spreads out as it travels, so at nine times the distance the same star would look about 75 times fainter. Antares actually looks brighter than ε, so it must give out hundreds of times more light.
card.wonder: The light from ε left about 64 years ago, while Antares' set out around the time the printing press was invented.
card.connect: ζ¹ Scorpii, farther down the tail, looks fainter still but outshines both by far.
card.answer: Because it is much closer: ε Scorpii is a modest giant next door and Antares a supergiant far away, and from here the two effects nearly cancel. How bright a star looks always mixes its true power with its distance.
card.photoCaption: The distance bar shows ε and Antares at their true depths behind the same patch of sky.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 51.19 ± 0.22 mas (≈64 ly) for this K1 III giant, against 5.89 ± 1.00 mas for Antares. With V ≈ 2.3 and 0.9 the distance ratio (≈8.7) implies Antares is roughly 250–300 times more luminous in visual light, before bolometric corrections that favor the cooler supergiant even more. ε Sco is not a member of the Upper Scorpius group: it is a foreground star.

distanceLy.note: dynamical distance 112 ± 5 pc; Hipparcos 2007 gives 5.71 ± 0.75 mas (≈570 ly)

massMsun.note: λ Sco A; B is 8.1 ± 1.0 M☉

components.label: B
components.notes: B star on a wide orbit resolved by interferometry

multiplicity.systemNote: Triple system (Tango et al. 2006); the WDS C component is a faint field star of unknown relation.

card.question: How do astronomers actually weigh a star?
card.glance: The bright blue-white stinger at the tip of Scorpius' tail, with fainter Lesath just beside it.
card.whyHere: Mass decides a star's whole life, yet you cannot put a star on a scale, and Shaula, the Scorpion's sting, is one of the systems that shows how it is done.
card.see: Follow the tail of Scorpius to its hook: the bright stinger is Shaula, with fainter Lesath just over half a degree west-south-west, both blue-white. Then sweep about five degrees north-east to the big, bright cluster M7.
card.understand: Shaula looks like one star but is at least three: two hot stars circling each other every few years, and a small third star whipping around the brightest every six days. Newton's law ties an orbit's size and period to the total mass inside it, so once you know how wide the orbit is and how long it takes, the mass follows. In 2006 an interferometer in Australia measured the wide orbit directly.
card.wonder: The brightest of the three also rings like a bell, swelling and shrinking slightly almost five times a day.
card.connect: M7, to the north-east, is a cluster so bright it was recorded in antiquity.
card.answer: Shaula's two main stars were weighed just this way, at about ten and eight Suns, from their motion around each other. The same orbit also gave the system's distance, which came out smaller than earlier estimates.
card.photoCaption: No photo separates the three stars; the binocular-field drawing shows Shaula and Lesath as the eye sees them.
card.notSee: All three stars of the system blur into one point at any small aperture.
card.deeper: Tango et al. (2006) resolved the A–B orbit with the Sydney University Stellar Interferometer: masses 10.4 ± 1.3 and 8.1 ± 1.0 M☉ and a dynamical distance of 112 ± 5 pc, about half the original Hipparcos value. Hipparcos 2007 gives 5.71 ± 0.75 mas (≈175 pc), so the distance is still disputed; the card range follows Tango. GCVS lists β Cephei pulsation with P = 0.2137 d and an amplitude of only 0.06 mag.

card.question: Where is the center of our Galaxy, and why can't we see it?
card.glance: The orange-tinted tip of the Teapot's spout; the Milky Way's brightest star clouds rise just above it.
card.whyHere: Everything you see tonight orbits a center you cannot see, and the Teapot's spout points almost straight at it.
card.see: Find the Teapot in Sagittarius and center its spout tip, Alnasl, a yellow-orange point. Sweep slowly west and north and the background thickens into rich star clouds broken by dark lanes; the Galaxy's center lies behind them about four and a half degrees west-north-west.
card.understand: Alnasl is a nearby orange giant, about 97 light-years away, a foreground lamp. Beyond it you are looking along the thickest part of the Milky Way's disk, through tens of thousands of light-years of stars and dust. Astronomers found the center by switching to light that dust cannot block: radio and infrared telescopes see straight through to a tight swarm of stars orbiting an invisible, heavy object.
card.wonder: Every star you have seen tonight, and the Sun with them, is orbiting that hidden point.
card.connect: The Lagoon Nebula, just above the spout, is a star nursery much nearer than the center.
card.answer: About four and a half degrees west-north-west of Alnasl, tens of thousands of light-years away, hidden behind thick dust; the glowing star clouds you see in that direction are only its foreground.
card.photoCaption: The binocular-field drawing marks the direction of the Galactic Center; nothing there is visible to the eye.
card.notSee: The Galactic Center itself is completely hidden by dust at visible wavelengths.
card.deeper: Alnasl (γ² Sgr, K0 III): Hipparcos 2007 parallax 33.67 ± 0.18 mas (≈97 ly). SIMBAD places the radio source Sgr A*, which marks the Galactic Center, at RA 17h45.7m, Dec −29.0°, 4.6° from γ² Sgr at position angle ≈287°. The visible Milky Way in this direction is dominated by foreground clouds such as the Sagittarius Star Cloud (M24).

card.question: How far does the Scorpius family of young stars spread?
card.glance: The brightest star of Lupus, a blue-white point low in the south for northern observers.
card.whyHere: The Scorpius stars are only the northern edge of a much larger family, and α Lupi belongs to one of its older branches.
card.see: Look low in the south, about thirty degrees south-west of Scorpius' head. Binoculars show a clean blue-white star in a rich, scattered field, and from mid-northern latitudes a clear southern horizon helps.
card.understand: α Lupi is a hot giant of the Upper Centaurus–Lupus group, siblings of the Scorpius stars born about 16 million years ago. Like many hot, heavy stars it gently pulses, about every six hours. The change is only a few hundredths of a magnitude, far too little for the eye.
card.wonder: This is the nearest family of hot young stars to the Sun.
card.connect: β and γ Lupi, its siblings, are scattered a few degrees away.
card.answer: Across a quarter of the southern sky: α Lupi belongs to an older branch of the same family.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the swatch shows its blue-white color.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 7.02 ± 0.17 mas (≈465 ly). GCVS: β Cephei type, V 2.29–2.34, P = 0.2598 d. A classic member of the Upper Centaurus–Lupus subgroup of Sco OB2 (de Zeeuw et al. 1999), median age about 16 Myr (Pecaut et al. 2012).

card.question: What happens to a family of stars after 16 million years?
card.glance: A blue-white star in Lupus, low in the south from mid-northern sites.
card.whyHere: Star families do not stay together forever, and β Lupi is a sibling already drifting away from its kin.
card.see: About five degrees north-east of α Lupi sits a steady blue-white point, the same color as α. Put both in one sweep and you have two family members side by side.
card.understand: β Lupi belongs to the Upper Centaurus–Lupus group, stars born together about 16 million years ago. Their birth cloud has long since dispersed, so nothing holds them together any more, and each drifts slowly along its own path. Astronomers still recognize the family by its shared motion and similar ages.
card.wonder: Its light left around the time Galileo died.
card.connect: γ Lupi, farther east, is a third sibling.
card.answer: It spreads out, and β Lupi and its siblings, no longer held by their birth cloud, are scattering across the southern sky.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the swatch shows its color.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 8.52 ± 0.18 mas (≈383 ly). Member of Upper Centaurus–Lupus (de Zeeuw et al. 1999).

card.question: Can one point of light be two young stars?
card.glance: A blue-white star at the eastern edge of Lupus; one point in binoculars.
card.whyHere: The third Lupus sibling adds a twist of its own: what binoculars show as one star is really two.
card.see: Look about ten degrees north-east of α Lupi. Binoculars show a single blue-white star, and its companion is far too close to split.
card.understand: γ Lupi is a close double of two hot young stars, both members of the Upper Centaurus–Lupus group. Heavy stars are usually born in pairs or small groups, so a double like this is the rule rather than the exception. Only telescopes reveal the second star.
card.wonder: Its light set out about four centuries ago, around when Kepler was working out how the planets move.
card.connect: Scorpius' head lies about twenty degrees to the north.
card.answer: γ Lupi is exactly that, two hot young stars too close for any binoculars to split, born together with the rest of the Lupus family.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the swatch shows its color.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 7.75 ± 0.50 mas (≈421 ly). Upper Centaurus–Lupus member (de Zeeuw et al. 1999). SIMBAD classes it as a double star.

card.question: What does a heavier Sun look like after its prime?
card.glance: The brightest star of Serpens, a pale orange point in binoculars.
card.whyHere: Unukalhai, the brightest star of Serpens, is a preview of later life for stars a little heavier than the Sun.
card.see: Center Unukalhai and defocus slightly to bring out its pale orange color. The globular cluster M5 lies about eight degrees to the south-west, an easy next hop.
card.understand: Unukalhai has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen into a giant. Its surface has cooled and reddened, but there is far more of it, so it shines much more brightly than it did in its prime. At 74 light-years it is a close neighbor as giants go.
card.wonder: Its light left about 74 years ago; M5's left long before there were people to see it.
card.connect: M5, south-west, is a far-off city of ancient stars.
card.answer: It swells, for once the core runs dry the outer layers balloon and cool, and the star becomes a pale orange giant like Unukalhai, far brighter than in its prime.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the swatch and HR diagram place it among the giants.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 44.10 ± 0.19 mas (≈74 ly). SIMBAD spectral type K2 IIIb CN1.

card.question: Why is one star of the Yed pair redder than the other?
card.glance: The orange-red member of the close naked-eye pair Yed in Ophiuchus.
card.whyHere: The naked-eye pair Yed gives you a ready-made color comparison, and the colors say something real.
card.see: Yed Prior and Yed Posterior sit about one and a half degrees apart in one binocular field, δ distinctly orange-red and ε yellower. That color difference is a temperature difference.
card.understand: δ Ophiuchi is a cool red giant near the end of its life, while ε is a warmer yellow giant. The cooler a star's surface, the more its light shifts toward red. The two are not partners at all, just a chance line-up at different distances.
card.wonder: Its light took about 170 years to arrive, its neighbor's about 110.
card.connect: 18 Scorpii, the Sun's near-twin, lies five degrees south.
card.answer: Because its surface is cooler: δ is the more swollen, more aged giant, and your eye reads the difference in temperature as color.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the swatch shows its orange-red color.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 19.06 ± 0.16 mas (≈171 ly); ε Oph (Gaia DR3 30.51 mas) is about 107 ly away, so the naked-eye 'pair' is optical. SIMBAD type M0.5 III.

card.question: Which star is the gateway to the Ophiuchus globular clusters?
card.glance: A bright white star in southern Ophiuchus; one point in binoculars.
card.whyHere: Ophiuchus is scattered with globular clusters, and Sabik is a bright, easy place to start hunting them.
card.see: Center Sabik, a crisp white point. About three and a half degrees to the south-east lies the faint globular M9, and several more globulars scatter across Ophiuchus.
card.understand: Sabik is two white stars orbiting each other, too close for binoculars, both in their steady hydrogen-burning years. It is only 88 light-years away. The globulars around it lie in the Galaxy's halo, hundreds of times deeper in space.
card.wonder: Its light left about 88 years ago, while light from the globulars around it has traveled for tens of thousands of years.
card.connect: M9 is the nearest of the Ophiuchus globulars.
card.answer: Sabik does the job, a bright, nearby pair that makes the ideal launch point for the globulars beyond it.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves the pair; the swatch shows its white color.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 36.91 ± 0.80 mas (≈88 ly). SIMBAD lists it as a double star (A2 IV-V); the pair is a telescope target.

card.question: Which star anchors the bottom of the Scorpion's head?
card.glance: The lowest of the three stars in Scorpius' head; a blue-white point.
card.whyHere: π Scorpii is another hot sibling of the Upper Scorpius family, and the yardstick for δ's wandering brightness.
card.see: π is the bottom star of the short arc formed with δ and β. Use it, with β, as a brightness yardstick for δ, whose light wanders.
card.understand: π Sco is a close pair of hot young stars, too tight for any telescope to split, revealed only by the way their spectral lines shift back and forth. Both belong to the Upper Scorpius group, about 11 million years old. Its own light barely flickers, which makes it a steady reference.
card.wonder: Its light has been traveling for about six centuries.
card.connect: δ, just above, may now be the brighter of the two.
card.answer: Fang, the lowest star of the head: a hot young pair that holds steady, the perfect yardstick for wandering δ.
card.photoCaption: No photo separates the pair; the swatch shows its color.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 5.57 ± 0.64 mas (≈590 ly). SIMBAD: B1 V + B2 V spectroscopic binary; GCVS lists a tiny eclipsing/ellipsoidal variation (Hp 2.82–2.85). Upper Sco member (de Zeeuw et al. 1999).

card.question: How different can two stars of the same family look?
card.glance: A blue-white star two degrees west-north-west of Antares, with M4 between them.
card.whyHere: Alniyat sits right beside Antares, a sibling of the same age that has taken a completely different path.
card.see: Put Antares at the edge of the field and look two degrees west-north-west for σ. M4's soft glow lies about a degree south-east of σ, between the two stars.
card.understand: σ Sco is a hot giant of the Upper Scorpius family that gently pulses about four times a day, changing by only a few hundredths of a magnitude. Antares was born heavier and has already swollen into a red supergiant. σ, lighter, is still blue-white.
card.wonder: A faint companion 20 arcseconds away is within reach of steady, mounted binoculars.
card.connect: Antares beside it: same family, same age, opposite colors.
card.answer: Blue-white σ Scorpii and orange-red Antares share a family and an age, yet look like strangers, because they differ in mass and therefore in stage of life.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the swatch shows its color.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 4.68 ± 0.60 mas (≈700 ly). GCVS: β Cephei type, V 2.86–2.94, P = 0.2468 d. WDS AB 20.5″ (V 2.9 and 8.4). Upper Sco member (de Zeeuw et al. 1999).

card.question: Is the Scorpion's second stinger star a partner of Shaula?
card.glance: The fainter of the two stinger stars at the tip of Scorpius' tail.
card.whyHere: Shaula's companion in the sting looks like its partner, which makes it a good test of how often the sky fools us.
card.see: Lesath sits just over half a degree west-south-west of Shaula. Both fit easily in one field, two blue-white points of unequal brightness.
card.understand: Lesath is a hot blue-white star about 576 light-years away. Shaula's own distance is still disputed, but the two are not bound together by gravity. They simply line up from Earth.
card.wonder: Its light left nearly six centuries ago, before Columbus sailed.
card.connect: M7 and M6 lie north-east of the sting.
card.answer: Lesath and Shaula share a direction, not an orbit, and only appear together from where we stand.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the binocular field drawing shows the stinger pair.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 5.66 ± 0.18 mas (≈576 ly). Shaula's distance is itself disputed (112 pc dynamical vs ≈175 pc Hipparcos 2007), so whether the two are close in space is unclear; they are not a bound pair.

card.question: Why is one star in Scorpius' blue tail yellow-white?
card.glance: A bright yellow-white star at the bottom of Scorpius' curling tail.
card.whyHere: Among the blue-white stars of Scorpius' tail, Sargas stands out with a warmer tone, a star in a different chapter of life.
card.see: At the lowest point of the tail's curl, Sargas shines yellow-white. Compare it with blue-white Shaula six degrees north: the difference is subtle but real.
card.understand: Sargas is an evolved star that has left its long hydrogen-burning phase. As its core contracted, its outer layers expanded and cooled. A cooler surface glows yellower, so its tint is a sign of age.
card.wonder: Its light took about three centuries to reach you, setting out in Isaac Newton's lifetime.
card.connect: The curl continues north to the stinger, Shaula.
card.answer: Sargas has aged, and past its hydrogen-burning prime it has swollen and cooled to yellow-white.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the swatch shows its yellow-white color.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 10.86 ± 1.49 mas (≈300 ly, ±14%). SIMBAD spectral type F1 III.

card.question: Which star in the Scorpion's tail quietly pulses five times a day?
card.glance: A blue-white star in the curl of Scorpius' tail, between Sargas and Shaula.
card.whyHere: The hot stars of Scorpius' tail are not perfectly steady, and Girtab is one that quietly rings like a bell.
card.see: Find κ about two and a half degrees south-east of Shaula, a single blue-white point. M7 lies about five degrees north-north-east.
card.understand: κ Sco is a hot giant whose surface swells and shrinks in a regular rhythm. Each pulse changes its light by only about a hundredth of a magnitude, far too little for the eye. Instruments time it precisely, and the rhythm reveals conditions deep inside the star.
card.wonder: Shaula, its neighbor in the sting, pulses in the same way.
card.connect: M7, north-north-east, is the brightest cluster in this part of the sky.
card.answer: That is Girtab, κ Scorpii, a hot giant whose tiny pulses repeat about five times a day.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the swatch shows its color.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 6.75 ± 0.17 mas (≈483 ly). GCVS: β Cephei type, V 2.41–2.42, P = 0.1998 d.

card.question: What does a heavy star look like in its swollen late stage?
card.glance: An orange star low in the far south, in Ara below Scorpius' tail.
card.whyHere: Ara, low below Scorpius' tail, holds a perfect pair of opposites, and β Arae is the old, swollen one.
card.see: Look below the tail of Scorpius, near the southern horizon. β Ara is a distinctly orange point, α Arae about six degrees north is blue-white, and the bright globular NGC 6397 lies about three degrees north-east.
card.understand: β Ara is a supergiant, a star several times heavier than the Sun that has swollen and cooled late in its life. Heavy stars race through their fuel, so it reached this stage while still young by the Sun's standards. Its orange glow comes from a surface cooler than the Sun's.
card.wonder: Its light left around the time of the Black Death in Europe.
card.connect: α Arae, in the same patch of sky, is a hot young star.
card.answer: It looks like β Arae, swollen, cooled and glowing orange, a supergiant in its last stages.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the swatch shows its orange color.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 5.05 ± 0.64 mas (≈650 ly); Gaia DR3 gives 4.56 ± 0.21 mas (≈715 ly). SIMBAD spectral type K0/1 Ib.

card.question: What happens when a star spins fast enough to shed gas?
card.glance: A blue-white star low in the south, the brightest point of Ara.
card.whyHere: δ Scorpii is not alone: α Arae is another hot star spinning fast enough to wrap itself in gas.
card.see: Find α Ara below Scorpius' tail, about six degrees north of orange β Arae. Side by side they make a lovely contrast, blue-white against orange.
card.understand: α Ara spins so fast that gas at its equator is barely held, and it has shed a flat disk of gas around its waist. The disk glows and adds light of its own. As the disk grows and thins, the star's brightness drifts slowly.
card.wonder: Its light took about 270 years to reach you, setting out around when Mozart was born.
card.connect: δ Scorpii shows the same kind of star in a showier mood.
card.answer: It wraps itself in its own gas: α Arae has shed a glowing disk around its equator, and its light wanders as the disk changes.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves the disk; the swatch shows the star's color.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 12.20 ± 0.85 mas (≈267 ly). GCVS: Be variable, 2.79–3.13 (B band). The 'ne' in B2Vne marks emission lines from the disk and broad lines from rapid rotation.

card.question: Are the Teapot's stars all at the same distance?
card.glance: The orange star at the middle of the Teapot's western side.
card.whyHere: The Teapot looks like a flat drawing, but its stars sit at very different depths, and Kaus Media is the farthest of the bright ones.
card.see: Kaus Media is the middle star on the spout side of the Teapot. Defocus slightly to see its orange tint, then compare it with blue-white Kaus Australis just below.
card.understand: Kaus Media is an orange giant about 350 light-years away. Kaus Borealis, at the top of the lid, is more than four times closer. The pattern only exists from our point of view.
card.wonder: Its light set out about three and a half centuries ago, around when Newton split sunlight into its colors with a prism.
card.connect: Kaus Australis, just below, is the Teapot's brightest star.
card.answer: The Teapot is a flat picture of a deep scene, and orange Kaus Media sits near the back of it.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the distance bar shows the Teapot's stars at their true depths.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 9.38 ± 0.18 mas (≈348 ly). SIMBAD spectral type K2.5 IIIa CN0.5.

card.question: How deep is the Teapot of Sagittarius?
card.glance: The brightest star of the Teapot, at its bottom corner; blue-white.
card.whyHere: The Teapot's brightest star makes a good reference for measuring how deep the whole pattern really is.
card.see: Kaus Australis marks the bottom of the Teapot, below Kaus Media. It is a crisp blue-white point beside that orange one.
card.understand: This hot star is about 143 light-years away. Measure the Teapot's other bright stars and they range from under 80 to about 350 light-years. Seen from elsewhere in the Galaxy, the pattern would fall apart.
card.wonder: Its light left around the time the first electric power stations opened.
card.connect: Ascella, at the east end of the base, sits beside a globular cluster.
card.answer: Several hundred light-years deep, with the brightest star, Kaus Australis, sitting partway back in that range.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the distance bar shows the Teapot in depth.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 22.76 ± 0.24 mas (≈143 ly). SIMBAD lists B9 IVp; it is a fast rotator with a faint close companion.

card.question: Which Teapot star opens the door to M22?
card.glance: The top of the Teapot's lid; an orange point with the globular M22 two and a half degrees away.
card.whyHere: The nearest bright star of the Teapot is also the doorway to one of the finest globular clusters in the sky.
card.see: Center the star at the top of the Teapot's lid. M22 lies about two and a half degrees north-east, a large round glow that binoculars begin to resolve at its edges under dark skies.
card.understand: Kaus Borealis is an orange giant only about 78 light-years away. M22 is a ball of hundreds of thousands of stars more than a hundred times farther. One short hop takes you from a neighbor to the Galaxy's halo.
card.wonder: Its light left about 78 years ago, while M22's left long before writing existed.
card.connect: M22 is one hop north-east.
card.answer: Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the lid: from there one short hop reaches M22.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the distance bar contrasts it with M22.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 41.72 ± 0.16 mas (≈78 ly). SIMBAD spectral type K1 IIIb. Near the ecliptic, so the Moon and planets sometimes pass close to it.

card.question: Which star guides you to the Teapot's globular clusters?
card.glance: The blue-white star at the top of the Teapot's handle.
card.whyHere: Nunki, at the top of the Teapot's handle, is the gateway to the globular clusters of eastern Sagittarius.
card.see: Nunki is the upper star of the handle, blue-white in binoculars. The globular M22 lies about five degrees west-north-west and M54 four degrees due south.
card.understand: Nunki is a hot star about 230 light-years away, much heavier than the Sun and still in its steady hydrogen-burning years. Its surface heat is what gives it that blue-white tint. Hot, heavy stars burn through their fuel fast, so by cosmic standards it will not keep this color for long.
card.wonder: Its light set out about 230 years ago, around the time of the French Revolution.
card.connect: Ascella and M54 lie south.
card.answer: Nunki, the handle's upper star, with a globular cluster a short hop away to the west and another to the south.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the swatch shows its color.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 14.32 ± 0.29 mas (≈228 ly). SIMBAD spectral type B2.5 V.

card.question: Can a star cluster belong to another galaxy?
card.glance: The white star at the bottom of the Teapot's handle, with the small globular M54 less than two degrees away.
card.whyHere: Beside Ascella lies one of the strangest objects in binocular range, a cluster that came from somewhere else.
card.see: Center Ascella, then look about 1.7 degrees west-south-west for M54, a small, faint fuzzy spot that needs a dark sky. In one sweep you go from 88 light-years to tens of thousands.
card.understand: Ascella is a close pair of white stars near us. M54 is thought to be the core of the Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy, a small galaxy now being torn apart and swallowed by the Milky Way. Its stars are strung out in streams that wrap around our Galaxy.
card.wonder: Ascella itself is a near neighbor whose light left about 88 years ago, so this field mixes our backyard with another galaxy's heart.
card.connect: M54's faint glow is right beside it.
card.answer: It can, and M54 is one: it arrived with the Sagittarius Dwarf, and as that galaxy is swallowed it will simply become another Milky Way globular.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves the pair; the distance bar contrasts Ascella with M54.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 36.98 ± 0.87 mas (≈88 ly). SIMBAD lists it as a double star (A2.5 Va); the pair is a telescope target.

card.question: Why does such a luminous star look so ordinary?
card.glance: A yellow-white star north-east of the Teapot's handle, distant and luminous.
card.whyHere: Albaldah looks like an everyday star above the Teapot's handle, which is exactly why it is worth a second look.
card.see: Albaldah sits several degrees north-east of Nunki, above the handle. It is a yellow-white point beside blue-white Nunki.
card.understand: Albaldah is an evolved bright giant, a star that has swollen past its steady phase to about 29 times the Sun's width. It pours out roughly 1,300 times the Sun's light, far more than the stars around it that look just as bright. So the reason it seems ordinary lies not in the star but in the space between us.
card.wonder: Its light left around the time of the Renaissance.
card.connect: The Teapot's handle and its globulars lie just south-west.
card.answer: It lies about 510 light-years away, and over that distance even great power fades to an ordinary point.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the swatch shows its color.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 6.40 ± 0.43 mas (≈510 ly). SIMBAD spectral type F2 II-III; listed as a multiple star.

card.question: Is the Terebellum a real group of stars?
card.glance: A yellowish star at a corner of the Terebellum, a small quadrilateral east of the Teapot.
card.whyHere: East of the Teapot lies a little-known box of stars, and ω Sagittarii at its corner shows that it is only a pattern.
card.see: Far east of the Teapot, look for four modest stars in a small box, the Terebellum; ω is its north-western corner. Binoculars show yellowish ω and the box's three other stars.
card.understand: ω Sgr is a yellow star a little further along in life than the Sun, beginning to leave its steady hydrogen-burning years. It is about 85 light-years away. The other three corners lie hundreds of light-years farther.
card.wonder: From there, our Sun would be too faint to see without binoculars.
card.connect: M55 and the Teapot lie back to the west.
card.answer: The Terebellum's four stars only line up from here, and ω Sagittarii has no true partner among them.
card.photoCaption: The survey photograph shows the field around ω Sgr.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 parallax 38.48 ± 2.66 mas (≈85 ly). SIMBAD spectral type G5 IV. WDS lists no wide companion (only a lunar-occultation pair), so the existing catalog's 'wide pair' description is not supported; the other Terebellum stars (59, 60, 62 Sgr) are unrelated, at roughly 370–860 ly (Gaia DR3).

contexts.name: Scorpius–Centaurus association (Sco OB2)
contexts.text: The nearest family of hot young stars to the Sun, spread over a quarter of the southern sky in three subgroups of slightly different ages.

contexts.name: Upper Scorpius
contexts.text: The youngest part of Sco-Cen: the head of Scorpius and Antares, next to the ρ Ophiuchi clouds where stars are still forming.

contexts.name: Upper Centaurus–Lupus
contexts.text: The middle, slightly older subgroup of Sco-Cen, strung through Lupus and the tail of Scorpius; ζ Oph was probably flung out of it by a supernova.

Antares has already aged into a cool red supergiant, while τ Scorpii, born alongside it, is still small, hot and blue-white.
edge.STAR-Antares>M4: Antares, about 11 million years old, shares one binocular field with M4, a globular cluster of stars roughly a thousand times older.
edge.HR6084>STAR-Antares: σ and Antares were born in the same Upper Scorpius family, yet one is still blue-white and the other has already turned red, because heavier stars age faster.
edge.HR5984>HR6027: β and ν Scorpii are both nests of several stars, and both belong to the young Upper Scorpius family.
edge.HR5984>HR5993: β's two stars truly travel together, while ω's two stars, one degree south, only look like a pair because they lie at very different distances.
edge.HR5953>HR5984: δ and β are neighbors in the head arc and siblings in the same family, so set them side by side and judge whether δ's glowing disk makes it the brighter tonight.
edge.HR5953>HR5944: π Scorpii, at the bottom of the head arc, is another Upper Scorpius sibling and a steady comparison star for δ.
edge.HR5953>HR6510: α Arae is another fast spinner wrapped in its own gas disk, the same physics as δ Scorpii in a calmer mood.
edge.HR6165>HR6175: Massive stars rarely live alone, and partners change their lives: τ may be two stars merged into one, while ζ Oph was flung away when its partner exploded.
edge.STAR-Antares>HR6175: Antares will one day explode, and ζ Ophiuchi shows what such a blast can do to a nearby star: it was kicked out of the Scorpius family when its partner went supernova.
edge.HR6175>HR5469: ζ Oph was probably born in the same Upper Centaurus–Lupus group as α Lupi, before a supernova sent it racing away.
edge.HR5469>HR5571: α and β Lupi are blue-white siblings of the Upper Centaurus–Lupus group, both about 16 million years old.
edge.HR5571>HR5776: γ Lupi is another member of the same Lupus family, which has now spread across several degrees of sky.
edge.HR6262>STAR-Antares: Two supergiants with opposite colors, {prev} giving out about {prevVal} and {next} about {nextVal}, and the blue one is both the heavier and by far the more luminous.
edge.HR6247>HR6262: The tail holds two naked-eye pairs: μ¹ and μ² are neighbors in space, but ζ¹ and ζ² are a trick of perspective, one forty times farther than the other.
edge.HR6241>STAR-Antares: ε Sco and Antares look similar in brightness, yet Antares is nearly nine times farther away, so it must make far more light.
edge.HR6241>HR6262: From about {prevVal} to about {nextVal}: ζ¹ looks fainter than ε but lies nearly a hundred times farther away.
edge.HR6527>M7: From a family of three stars in the sting to M7, a family of dozens you can count one by one in binoculars.
edge.HR6527>HR6580: Shaula and κ Scorpii both pulse every few hours, like bells ringing too faintly to hear.
edge.HR6461>HR6510: Side by side in Ara sit orange β, a swollen supergiant, and blue-white α, a hot star spinning fast.
edge.HR6461>NGC6397: From a heavy star living fast to one of the oldest and nearest globular clusters, only three degrees away.
edge.HR6247>HR5586: δ Librae is another pair that eclipses itself, with a deeper and slower dip than μ¹'s.
edge.DS-AlpLib>HR5685: The two claws of Libra look almost equally bright, but β is more than twice as far away as α, so it must shine several times more strongly.
edge.DS-AlpLib>HR5586: α Librae's partners are wide enough to split, while δ Librae's are so close that we know of them only because they eclipse each other.
edge.HR5685>STAR-Antares: {prev} at about {prevVal} and {next} at about {nextVal}: color is a thermometer, and green-rumored Zubeneschamali sits at its hot, blue-white end.
edge.HD140283>M5: HD 140283 is a lone traveler from the Galaxy's youth, and M5 is a whole city of stars of similar age.
edge.HD140283>HR6060: Two Sun-like stars from two eras: HD 140283 formed when the Galaxy was nearly free of heavy elements, and 18 Sco, like the Sun, billions of years later from enriched gas.
edge.HR6060>HR6056: 18 Sco shows the Sun as it is now, and five degrees north Yed Prior shows the swollen red giant stage that awaits stars like it.
edge.HR6060>HR6401: From a twin of the Sun to a family of slightly smaller, cooler orange suns next door.
edge.HR5854>M5: From an orange giant about 74 light-years away to M5, a globular cluster hundreds of times farther.
edge.HR6401>M62: From one of the Sun's close neighbors, about {prevVal} away, to a globular cluster roughly a thousand times farther, in a single sweep.
edge.HR6401>M19: Three degrees west, M19 lies more than a thousand times farther away than 36 Oph.
edge.HR6401>STAR-Antares: Both are orange, but 36 Oph is a modest dwarf about 19 light-years away and Antares a supergiant almost thirty times farther, a candle close by against a lighthouse far away.
edge.HR6378>M9: From Sabik, under a hundred light-years away, to the faint globular M9, hundreds of times farther.
edge.HR6736>NGC6530: NGC 6530, just east of 9 Sgr, is the Lagoon's young cluster, born from the same cloud.
edge.HR6746>M24: From a foreground lamp 97 light-years away to a star cloud thousands of light-years deep along the Milky Way's disk.
edge.HR6746>M8: Just above the spout, the Lagoon Nebula lies dozens of times farther away than the spout star itself.
edge.HR6913>M22: From the Teapot's lid, under a hundred light-years away, to M22, a globular cluster more than a hundred times farther.
edge.HR7194>M54: Less than two degrees separate a star 88 light-years away from a cluster that belongs to another galaxy, the Sagittarius dwarf.
edge.HR6859>HR6913: The Teapot is flat only on the sky: Kaus Media lies about four and a half times farther away than Kaus Borealis at the top of the lid.
edge.HR6879>HR6859: Blue-white Kaus Australis and orange Kaus Media sit one above the other, a hot star and a cool giant in the same pattern.
edge.HR7121>M54: Four degrees south of Nunki lies M54, hundreds of times farther away than the handle star.
edge.DS-OmSgr>M55: From a nearby yellow star to M55, a loose globular cluster about two hundred times farther away.
